source: OKOA Investor Portal design/security/SECURITY-PROTOCOL.md (byte copy in rulebook/)
rule_zero: Security is the most important property of anything built under this protocol. There is no trade-off that buys a loophole. If a feature cannot be built securely in the time available, the feature waits; the loophole never ships.

principles.title: Deny by default.
principles.text: Nothing is readable, writable or callable until a rule explicitly allows it for that person, that row, that action. Row-level security on every table; a table without a policy shows nothing. Every endpoint starts closed.

principles.title: Least privilege, everywhere.
principles.text: People, services, database roles, API keys and build agents each get the smallest set of rights that lets them do their one job. Staff bypass is a named role, never the default connection.

principles.title: Defense in depth.
principles.text: The application checks, the database checks again, the audit log records it, and a test proves it. One layer failing must not expose data.

principles.title: Never trust input.
principles.text: Every value that crosses a boundary (browser, file, e-mail, API, another skill, an AI model) is validated against an allow-list and encoded on output.

principles.title: Data minimization.
principles.text: Collect, store, show, log and send only what the feature needs. Mask by default (last-4). Encrypt sensitive values before they reach storage.

principles.title: Fail closed.
principles.text: When unsure, refuse with a typed error and log it. Never guess, never fall back to "show everything", never swallow an error.

principles.title: Separation of duties.
principles.text: The person who writes a thing is not the person who approves it: code review, report approval, campaign send, payment-like actions.

principles.title: Everything on record.
principles.text: Every change, login, denial, export and impersonation is in an append-only audit trail that the actor cannot edit.

principles.title: No secrets in code, prompts, logs or tickets.
principles.text: Secrets live in a secrets manager or environment injection; the repository, the transcript and the model never see them.

principles.title: Reproducible and reviewed.
principles.text: Pinned dependencies, lockfiles, signed releases, branch protection, and an independent adversarial review before anything reaches people.

principles.title: No fabricated security.
principles.text: A claim like "this is safe" without a test, a record and a reviewer is not a claim; it is a guess. Say "unverified" when it is unverified.

principles.title: Humans approve the irreversible.
principles.text: Deletes of real data, sends to real people, and any money-like action need a second person and a confirmation step.

steps.title: Pre-task security check — before anything else
body: Before the first file is opened, write the task's threat sketch (template in Part 4):
Gate: no threat sketch → the task does not start.
bullets: What data does this touch? Classify it (Part 3.6): public / internal / confidential / sensitive (PII, financial, secrets).
Who may see or change it? Name the roles and the row-level rule.

What could go wrong? Walk STRIDE: Spoofing (fake identity), Tampering (changed data), Repudiation (no record), Information disclosure (leak), Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. One line each, "none" allowed only with a reason.
What is the abuse case? Write the attacker's story in two sentences.

steps.title: Design review — before code
body: Gate: design review recorded (Part 4) → coding may start.
bullets: Draw the data flow: where the data enters, where it is stored, where it leaves, and every trust boundary it crosses.
Write the authorization matrix for the feature: rows = actions, columns = roles, cells = allowed / denied / own-rows-only. The row-level-security rule for each table is written here.
Decide the typed errors the feature returns (PERMISSION_DENIED, NOT_FOUND, VALIDATION_FAILED, …) and that they never leak existence of other people's data.
Decide what is logged and what must never be logged (secrets, full tax ids, full bank numbers, session tokens, raw request bodies with PII).
If an AI model is involved: what exactly goes into the prompt, what must never go in, and who approves the output before anyone else sees it.

steps.title: The line rule — while writing
body: Before every line of code (or SQL, or config) is committed to the file, answer the twelve
questions silently; if any answer is "yes", write the line differently or stop and fix the cause:
1. Does this line read or write data without the caller's authorization being checked on this
2. Does it build a query, a command, HTML, a URL or an e-mail from input without
3. Does it trust a client-supplied id, role, price, amount, profile or user id?
4. Does it log, print, return or store a secret, a full sensitive value, or more fields than needed?
5. Does it catch an error and continue as if nothing happened?
6. Does it widen a permission, a CORS rule, a role, a policy, or disable a check "for now"?
7. Does it use randomness, hashing or encryption from a hand-rolled or non-approved source?
8. Does it accept a file, a path, a redirect target, an HTML fragment or a template from input
9. Does it send data to a third party, a model, a webhook or an e-mail that the design review
10. Does it depend on a package, version or script that is not pinned and reviewed?
11. Does it make an irreversible or money-like action without the second-person step?
12. Could this line behave differently under concurrency, retries or a replayed request
If the problem comes from somewhere else (a missing policy, an upstream function that
returns too much, a library default), the line is not the place to patch it: open the real cause
as a security issue (Part 4) and fix it there, now, before continuing. Do not "write around" an
upstream hole.

steps.title: Post-change scan — after every change
body: Run all of these; record the results:
bullets: Static checks: type-check, lint with security rules, secret scanner over the diff and the repository, dependency audit (known vulnerabilities), license and provenance check for new packages.
Policy check: every new table has row-level security enabled; every new view runs as the caller; every new endpoint has an authorization test; every new write path has a typed error path.

Tests: the feature's positive tests and its negative tests: wrong user, wrong row, wrong role, missing field, oversized input, replay, concurrent duplicate. A feature with no negative test is not done.
Data tests: no sensitive value appears in logs, error messages, exports or test fixtures that leave the machine.
Review the diff as an attacker: read every changed line asking the twelve questions again.

steps.title: The iterative fix loop — until zero
body: Every finding from S3 (or from a reviewer, a scanner, a holdout, or production) enters the
issue list with a severity (Part 2, "Severity"). Then:
repeat
until the list has zero open issues
then run S3 once more; it must be clean twice in a row
The loop has no step budget. Stopping with an open issue is a defect, whatever its severity.
A finding may be closed only by a fix plus a passing re-check, or by a written decision from
the owner that the finding is a false positive, with the reason.

steps.title: The security check record — written evidence
body: Each task ends with a record (template in Part 4) that lists: the threat sketch, the design
review, the issues found and how each was closed, the scans run and their results, the tests
added, the reviewer, and the leftover risks with owners and dates. No record → not done.

steps.title: Independent adversarial review
body: A second reviewer who did not write the code (a person, or a separate Claude agent with no
shared context) reads the change and the record with one goal: break it. The reviewer reports
findings in the same severity scale; the loop in S4 runs again on them.

steps.title: Holdout proof
body: For every security-relevant behavior, a holdout test written before the code and hidden from
the builder (see `acos-holdout-test`) proves the behavior at reveal time: cross-user reads are
denied, soft-deleted rows never render, exports are logged, drafts are invisible, approvals need
a second person. A holdout that blocks is a security issue.

steps.title: Release gate and watch
body: Before release: zero open security issues at any severity, S6 complete, holdouts passed, secrets
rotated if any were exposed during the work, backups and restore tested, monitoring and alerts
in place for failed logins, permission denials, rate limits and unusual exports. After release:
the alerts are read, and every incident re-enters the loop at S0.

twelve_questions: Does this line read or write data without the caller's authorization being checked on this row?
Does it build a query, a command, HTML, a URL or an e-mail from input without parameterization or encoding?
Does it trust a client-supplied id, role, price, amount, profile or user id?
Does it log, print, return or store a secret, a full sensitive value, or more fields than needed?
Does it catch an error and continue as if nothing happened?
Does it widen a permission, a CORS rule, a role, a policy, or disable a check "for now"?
Does it use randomness, hashing or encryption from a hand-rolled or non-approved source?
Does it accept a file, a path, a redirect target, an HTML fragment or a template from input without an allow-list?
Does it send data to a third party, a model, a webhook or an e-mail that the design review did not list?
Does it depend on a package, version or script that is not pinned and reviewed?
Does it make an irreversible or money-like action without the second-person step?
Could this line behave differently under concurrency, retries or a replayed request (double payout, double send)?

severity.meaning: Data of another person readable or changeable; secrets exposed; money-like action without control
severity.rule: Stop all other work. Fix now.

severity.meaning: A control missing that one more mistake would turn into Critical (no RLS on a table, no negative test, no audit)
severity.rule: Fix before the change is merged.

severity.meaning: Weakens a layer (verbose error, missing rate limit, loose validation)
severity.rule: Fix before the feature is called done.

severity.meaning: Hygiene (header missing, stale dependency without known exploit)
severity.rule: Fix in the same task; may not be deferred past release.

items.text: Login is delegated to a proven provider (e.g. Clerk) or a reviewed library; no home-made password storage.
Multi-factor is available and required for staff.
Sessions expire; logout invalidates server-side; tokens are not in localStorage; cookies are HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite.
Invitations are single-use, expire, and bind to the invited e-mail.
Sign-up or activation that needs staff approval stays in a pending state that can read nothing.
Failed logins and lockouts are logged and rate-limited.
Every table has row-level security enabled; staff bypass is a named role.
Every view runs as the caller (security_invoker).
Every endpoint checks authorization on the object, not only on the role (no IDOR).
Investors (or end users) can write only their own rows in a short, listed set of tables.
Impersonation ("view as") is a logged, time-boxed, read-only mode.
Permission denials return the same shape as "not found" where existence must not leak.
Parameterized queries only; no string-built SQL, shell, LDAP or template code.
HTML from users or AI is sanitized with an allow-list; rendered content never executes scripts.
Output is encoded for its context (HTML, attribute, URL, JSON, CSV formula injection).
File uploads: allow-listed types, size limit, content sniffed, stored outside the web root under a generated name, served through signed, expiring URLs, scanned where possible.
Redirects and links only to allow-listed destinations.
Numbers for money are decimal, never float; parsing rejects anything but digits, sign and point.
Secrets come from the environment or a secrets manager; .env files are ignored by git.
A secret scanner runs on every commit; a found secret is rotated, not just removed.
Production, staging and development have separate secrets and separate data.
Debug modes, verbose errors and sample accounts are off in production.
TLS everywhere; HSTS on.
Sensitive fields are encrypted by the application with a managed key before storage; only a last-4 is kept in clear.
Keys are rotated on a schedule and on any suspicion; old keys can still decrypt.
Only well-known libraries; no custom algorithms; strong randomness for ids, tokens, invites.
Public / internal / confidential / sensitive, decided in S0 and written on the schema (sensitive flag) and the API.
Sensitive data is masked in every list and export unless the viewer has an explicit right.
Exports (PDF, CSV, Excel, images) are logged with who, what, filters and size.
Retention: what is kept how long, and how it is deleted (soft delete first, purge on schedule).
The person's own rights: view, correct, export, erase where the law applies.
Append-only audit table for inserts, updates, deletes, logins, failed logins, denials, rate limits, exports, downloads, impersonation, invites.
Logs never contain secrets, full sensitive values, session tokens or full request bodies.
Audit rows record the acting user and any "acting as" identity.
Logs are time-synchronized, retained, and alert on patterns (many denials, mass export).
Sending domain has SPF, DKIM and DMARC; the sender is a fixed list.
Templates are allow-listed merge fields; no raw HTML from input.
Links are to our domain, expire where they grant access, and never carry secrets in the URL.
Bulk sends need a second-person approval and a test send first.
Unsubscribe and bounce handling exist and are honored.
The model sees the minimum: one person's data for one output; never secrets; never other people's rows.
Prompts are templates with validated slots; user text is marked as data, never as instruction (prompt injection defense); tool access is allow-listed.
Model output is treated as untrusted input: sanitized, validated, and approved by a person before anyone else sees it.
Every generation is recorded (model, instruction hash, input hash), without storing the raw prompt that contained personal data.
No external model endpoint receives confidential data unless the contract and the data-flow review allow it; subscription-bound agents preferred where available.
CSRF protection on state-changing requests; CORS allow-list; security headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, frame-ancestors).
Rate limits per user and per IP on login, requests, exports, searches; limits are logged.
Pagination caps; no unbounded list endpoints.
Idempotency keys on anything that could be replayed (sends, postings, approvals).
Lockfile committed; versions pinned; new packages reviewed (purpose, maintainer, size, install scripts).
Automated vulnerability audit in CI; a known exploitable vulnerability blocks.
Builds are reproducible from a clean checkout; no network fetches at runtime from unpinned sources; CDN scripts pinned to exact versions and allow-listed by CSP.
Branch protection: review required, CI green required, no force-push to main.
RLS on every table; policies tested with a negative test per table.
Soft delete and audit on business tables; immutable (append-only) tables for ledgers and events.
Constraints carry the invariants (checks, uniques, foreign keys) so bad data cannot be stored.
Migrations are reviewed with the twelve questions; destructive migrations need a backup first.
Backups encrypted, tested by an actual restore, and access-logged.
Private network for the database; least-privilege roles; no shared admin accounts.
Encryption at rest; key management by the provider or a KMS.
Monitoring and alerts; an incident runbook; a contact for security reports.
Access to production data is logged and needs a reason.
No sensitive data in localStorage or in URLs; only per-viewer conveniences.
Strict CSP; no inline event handlers; dependencies pinned; subresource integrity where used.
Clickjacking protection; forms with CSRF tokens; file downloads via signed URLs.
Accessibility of security flows (every action possible without a mouse).

templates.threat_sketch:
task: <id / title>
data_touched: [<table or object>: <public|internal|confidential|sensitive>, ...]
actors: [<role>: <what they may do>, ...]
stride:
  spoofing: <one line or "none because ...">
  tampering: <...>
  repudiation: <...>
  information_disclosure: <...>
  denial_of_service: <...>
  elevation_of_privilege: <...>
abuse_case: <two sentences from the attacker's view>
checklists: [3.1, 3.2, 3.3, ...]
templates.design_review:
data_flow: <entry -> storage -> exit; trust boundaries named>
authorization_matrix:
  - action: <...>; staff: allow; investor: own_rows; anonymous: deny
rls_rules: [<table>: <policy in words>, ...]
typed_errors: [PERMISSION_DENIED, NOT_FOUND, VALIDATION_FAILED, ...]
logging: {log: [...], never_log: [...]}
ai_use: {inputs: [...], never_inputs: [...], approver: <role>}  # or "none"
reviewer: <who>
templates.security_issue:
id: SEC-<n>
severity: critical|high|medium|low
found_by: scan|test|review|holdout|production
where: <file:line or table/policy or endpoint>
what: <one sentence>
root_cause: <one sentence — the real cause, not the symptom>
fix: <what changed>
re_check: <scan/test run after the fix, and its result>
closed_at: <date>   # only after a clean re-check

short_version: Nothing starts without a threat sketch.
Deny by default; every table has row-level security; every view runs as the caller.
Ask the twelve questions before every line; fix causes, not symptoms.
Scan, test (negative tests too), and re-scan after every fix, until clean twice.
Write the record; get the adversarial review; pass the holdout.
Zero open issues at release — at every severity. No loophole, ever.
